newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania needs action on Moldova ties, says premier.
newsitem.headline: Romania needs action on Moldova ties, says premier.

text.p: Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea said on Thursday that Romania needed concrete action rather than a restatement of common heritage to develop ties with the neighbouring former Soviet republic of Moldova.

"It is time to move from the phase of flower bridges to the phase of concrete and steel bridges," Ciorbea told reporters after talks with his Moldovan opposite number, Ion Ciubuc. "We should stop talking and start dealing with facts."

Ciorbea was referring to emotional rallies held across the border between Romanians and ethnic Romanians in Moldova, starting in the final two years of Soviet rule. When border points were closed, demonstrators threw flowers into the Prut river separating the two countries.
Moldova is mostly made up of former Romanian territory seized by the Kremlin under the 1939 Nazi-Soviet pact and 60 percent of its 4.3 million people are ethnic Romanians.
Calls for reunification with Romania enjoyed considerable backing after the end of Soviet rule, but are now confined to a tiny nationalist minority on both sides of the border.

Ciorbea told reporters bilateral trade, currently in Romania's favour but never more than $180 million annually since 1992, could eventually be used as a bridge between western Europe and the former Soviet Union.
"Our talks stressed that Romania can act as a gateway to Europe for Moldovan goods and Moldova as a gateway to former Soviet republics for Romanian goods," he said.
Ciorbea also said Romania had asked Moldova to invest in construction of a second reactor at the Canadian-built Cernavoda nuclear power station in southeastern Romania.

Both leaders said talks were under way on completing a post-Soviet treaty. Romania is expected to sign a similar pact with neighbouring Ukraine next month, vital for its longshot bid for early NATO membership, after dropping demands for Kiev to atone for the Soviet seizure of former Romanian territory.
Ciubuc sidestepped a question from one journalist who asked whether he thought the two neighbours would ever reunite.
"Our aim is for people on both sides of the Prut to live in prosperity and stability," he said.
